claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has low hardness and strength.
The alloy lacks significant lattice distortions.
The alloy contains a weak grain-boundary network.
A lack of significant lattice distortions facilitates dislocation movement.
A weak grain-boundary network facilitates grain-boundary sliding.
Easy dislocation movement and grain-boundary sliding govern the alloy's low hardness and strength.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature under uniaxial tensile loading.
High-entropy alloys with significant lattice distortions and strong grain-boundary networks provide the baseline comparison.
Grain-boundary engineering can be used to create a controlled comparison with the starting CoCrFeNiTi state.
Hardness, strength, and grain-boundary character distribution are measurable observables for the proposed comparison.
Significantly improved hardness and strength after grain-boundary engineering would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes low hardness and strength partly to a weak grain-boundary network, so improving the grain-boundary network and observing increased hardness and strength would support that causal account rather than falsify it. A falsifying result would instead be no relevant property or deformation change despite a verified change in grain-boundary character, or evidence that the proposed deformation modes are not operative.
